To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The most common reasons for not washing hands were that it was not convenient or that it was not necessary; 2) Nurses were more likely to wash their hands if the patient was in isolation; and 3) Nurses were more compliant with hand washing when the patient was in a private room than when the patient was sharing a room.

hand hygiene noncompliant behavior is influenced by a complex set of factors, and that the determinants of hand hygiene compliance are different for physicians, nurses, and ancillary health care workers.

the most important determinants of hand hygiene compliance in ICUs are (i) the presence of a hand hygiene promotion program, (ii) nurses’ perceptions of the importance of hand hygiene, (iii) the number of hand hygiene opportunities, (iv) the presence of alcohol-based hand rub dispensers, and (v) nurses’ perceptions that their work environment is safe and supportive.

hand hygiene compliance in intensive care units is a multifaceted issue that can be affected by many factors.

hand hygiene noncompliances in ICUs are multifactorial.
the most important factors for noncompliance with hand hygiene in intensive care units were related to the work environment and were not related to the staff.
